Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 1–3:

The interpretation of His, may His praise be exalted, saying: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded (1) Those who are humble in their prayer (2) And those who turn away from vain talk (3)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, may His praise be exalted, saying ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ He means: those who believed in God and His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), acknowledged what came to them from God, and acted upon what he called them to, as named in these verses, have attained eternal abiding in the gardens of their Lord, and have achieved their desires with Him.

As follows:

* Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾, then said: Ka'b said: God did not create anything with His own hand except three: He created Adam with His hand, He wrote the Torah with His hand, and He planted the Garden of Eden with His hand. Then He said to it: "Speak!" So it said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾, because of the honour He knew would be in it.

* Sahl ibn Musa al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn al-Daris narrated to us, from Amr ibn Abi Qays, from Abd al-Aziz ibn Rufay', from Mujahid, who said: When God, blessed and exalted, planted the Garden, He looked at it and said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾.

* He said: Hafs ibn Umar narrated to us, from Abu Khaldah, from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: When God created the Garden He said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾, and then sent down the Qur'an with it.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jubayr narrated to us, from Ata', from Maysarah, who said: "God did not create anything with His hand except four things: He created Adam with His hand, He wrote the Tablets with His hand, the Torah with His hand, and He planted Eden with His hand. Then He said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾."

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: those who, when they stand in their prayer, are humble. Their humility in it is their submission to God within it through obeying Him, and their standing in it with what He commanded them to uphold therein. It was said that this was revealed because the people used to raise their eyes toward the sky during prayer before it was revealed, so they were forbidden from that by this verse.

Narrations to this effect:

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed, he would look toward the sky, and then this verse was revealed: ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾. He said: After that he would direct his face to where he prostrated."

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Harun ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Hajjaj al-Sawwaf, from Ibn Sirin, who said: "The companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to raise their eyes in prayer toward the sky, until it was revealed: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer﴾. Then they said: after that, with their heads like this."

* Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: Ayyub informed us, from Muhammad, who said: "I was told that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed he would raise his gaze to the sky, and a verse was revealed: if it was not ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, then I do not know which verse it is. He said: So he lowered his head." He said: Muhammad also said: "They used to say: one should not let his gaze pass beyond his prayer place, and if he has become accustomed to looking, let him close his eyes."

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Ibn Awn, from Muhammad, similarly.

The interpreters differed regarding what is meant by humility here. Some of them said: it means stillness of the limbs in prayer.

Those who said this:

* Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid: ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, he said: stillness within it.

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri: ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, he said: a person's stillness in his prayer.

* Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, the same.

* Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from al-Thawri, from Abu Sufyan al-Shaybani, from a man, from Ali, who said: he was asked about His saying ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, and said: Do not turn your head during your prayer.

* Abd al-Jabbar ibn Yahya al-Ramli narrated to us, saying: Damrah ibn Rabi'ah said, from Abu Shawdhab, from al-Hasan, concerning His saying ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, he said: their humility was in their hearts, so by it they lowered their gaze and lowered their wing.

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim, concerning His saying ﴿humble﴾, he said: the humility is in the heart, and he said: still.

* He said: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn Abd Allah narrated to me, from al-Mas'udi, from Abu Sinan, from a man of his people, from Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: Humility is in the heart, and that you lower your side for the Muslim person, and do not turn around.

* He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said, concerning His saying ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾: it is taking on humility in prayer. And someone other than Ata' said to me: the Prophet (ﷺ) when he stood in prayer would look to his right, his left, and in front of him, until it was revealed: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer﴾, and after that he was never seen looking except at the ground.

Others said: it means fear in this place.

Those who said this:

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan: ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, he said: fearful.

* Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, concerning His saying ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, al-Hasan said: fearful. And Qatadah said: humility is in the heart.

* Ali narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, he said: fearful and still.

We have already explained earlier in our book that humility is submission and lowliness, in a manner sufficient to not repeat it here. Since this is so, and God, may His remembrance be exalted, has not indicated by reason or report that His intent is one meaning over another, it is known that the meaning of His intent is generality. Since this is so, the interpretation of the speech is what I have described before: that those who are in their prayer are humbled before God by continuing what He obligated them of His obligation and worship, and when the servant is humbled before God within it, the humility of his submission is seen in the stillness of his limbs and his occupation with His obligation and his leaving what he was commanded to leave within it.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: and those who turn away from falsehood and what God dislikes among His creatures.

The interpreters said similarly to what we have said regarding its interpretation.

Those who said this:

* Ali narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾, he said: falsehood.

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan: ﴿turn away from vain talk﴾, he said: from sins.

* Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, the same.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾, he said: the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him of his companions, who believed in him, followed him and affirmed him, were "turning away from vain talk."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verses 4–7:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And those who are constant in giving zakah (zakat)﴾ [23:4], ﴿and those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blamed. But whoever seeks beyond that, then it is those who are the transgressors﴾ [23:5–7].

His, the Exalted's, mention means: And those who pay the zakah of their wealth which Allah has enjoined upon them, and their action by which they are described is their paying it.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives﴾

He says: And those who guard their private parts. By "private parts" in this place is meant the private parts of men, and that is their genitals. ﴿Guarding﴾ them means they keep them from their acts in any of the private parts. ﴿Except from their wives﴾ means: except with their wives whom Allah has made lawful to men through marriage. ﴿Or those their right hands possess﴾ means by that: their female slaves. The "ma" in His saying ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾ is in the genitive position, conjoined to "wives" (al-azwaj). ﴿For indeed they are not blamed﴾ means: for indeed whoever does not guard his private part from his wife and the one his right hand possesses, but guards it from others of creation, then he is not reproached for that, nor censured, nor by his doing that is he committing a sin for which he is blamed.

And according to what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said.

Mention of those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to us, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blamed﴾: He means: Allah has approved for them their going to their wives and what their right hands possess.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿Those who will inherit al-Firdaws﴾, he said: al-Firdaws: a garden in Roman (Greek) language.

He said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, who said: 'Adn is a garden in Paradise, its palace therein is 'Adn, which He created with His hand. It opens every dawn and He looks at it, then says: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾. He said: That garden is also al-Firdaws. Mujahid said: God planted it with His hand, and when it was complete He said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾. Then He commanded that it be closed, so no creation nor any near angel looks into it. Then it opens every pre-dawn, and He looks into it and says: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾. Then it is closed again until its like.

⁕ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: Harithah ibn Suraqah was killed on the day of Badr, and his mother said: O Messenger of God, if my son is among the people of Paradise, I will not weep for him; and if he is among the people of the Fire, I will weep excessively. He said: "O mother of Harithah, there are two gardens within Paradise, and your son has attained al-Firdaws al-A'la (the highest Paradise)."

⁕ al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to me, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from Ka'b, who said: God created the Garden of al-Firdaws with His hand and planted it with His hand. Then He said: Speak! It said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾.

⁕ He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Hassam ibn Mistak, from Qatadah also, the like of it, except that he said: Speak! It said: "Blessed (tuba) for the God-fearing."

⁕ He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yazid narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Dawud Nafi', who said: When God created it, He said to it: Adorn yourself; so it adorned itself. Then He said to it: Speak! It said: "Blessed is he with whom You are pleased."

* *

As for His words: ﴿therein they will abide eternally﴾

That is, they will remain therein. He says: those who inherit al-Firdaws are eternal, meaning they remain therein forever, not moving away from it.

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾ (12)**

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾, meaning: We extracted him from it. The *sulālah* (extract) is what is drawn out of any soil, and for this reason Adam was created from earth taken from the surface of the ground.

In agreement with what we have said, the people of *ta'wīl* (interpretation of the Qur'an) differed about who is meant by "man" in this passage. Some of them said that it refers to Adam.

Those who said this:

- Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding ﴿from clay﴾: He said: Adam was extracted from clay.

- al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding His words ﴿from an extract of clay﴾: He said: Adam was extracted from clay, and his offspring were created from a contemptible fluid.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: And We did certainly create the offspring of Adam, who is the man mentioned in this passage, from an extract, which is the drop of semen that is drawn out from the loins of the stallion (male), from clay, and that is Adam, who was created from clay.

Those who said this:

- al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Abū Muʿāwiyah narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhāl ibn ʿAmr, from Abū Yaḥyā, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿from an extract of clay﴾: He said: the choice (essence) of the water.

- Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding God's words (*min sulālah*, "from an extract"): from the semen of Adam.

- al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, the like of it.

The more correct of the two views regarding this matter is the view of the one who said: its meaning is: And We did certainly create the son of Adam from an extract of Adam, which is the essence of his water (semen), and Adam is the clay, because he was created from it.

We said that this is the more apt of the two interpretations of the verse because of the indication of His words ﴿Then We placed him as a drop in a firm lodging﴾, which shows that this is so, since it is known that he did not come to be in a firm lodging except after being created in the loins of the stallion (male), and after being transferred from his loins he came to be in a firm lodging. The Arabs call a man's offspring and his drop (semen) *sulālah* and *salīl*, because both are drawn out from him. From the word *sulālah* is the saying of one of them:

*They carried him, a sharp-skinned, lion-like [child], an extract of a vagina that was not guarded.* [[The verse is by Ḥassān ibn Thābit (Lisān: s-l-l), and in it the wording is "fa-jāʾat" in place of "ḥamalat." It is evidence that *sulālah* means the drop of a human being, and that the *sulālah* of a thing is what is drawn out of it. The author cited it as evidence that the Arabs call a man's offspring and his drop *sulālah*. In the Lisān: al-Farrāʾ said: *sulālah* is that which is drawn from every soil. Abū al-Haytham said: *sulālah* is what is drawn from the loins of a man and the ribs of a woman, just as a thing is drawn out (*yusallu*) by drawing (*sallan*). The *salīl* is the child at the moment it emerges from its mother's womb, because it was created from the *sulālah*. ʿIkrimah said regarding *sulālah*: it is the water drawn from the back by drawing. *ʿAḍab al-adīm* means thick-skinned; perhaps he intends to describe him with strength and harshness. I did not find this expression in the lexicon books, but I found it in a marginal note on a photographed copy of Majāz al-Qurʾān kept in the Cairo University library, number 26059, at the commentary on God's words: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾.]]

And the saying of another:

*Was I anything but a filly of Arab (noble) stock, an extract of mares covered by a mule?* [[The verse is by Hind bint al-Nuʿmān (Lisān: s-l-l), and its transmitted wording is "Wa-mā Hind illā mahratan." It is evidence that *salīl* means a child, and the feminine is *salīlah*. Abū ʿAmr said: *salīlah* is a man's daughter from his loins. *Tajallalahā* means covered her (mounted her). The "mule" here means a man resembling a mule, and the mule is blameworthy among the Arabs. In the Lisān: s-l-l: Ibn Barrī said: some of them mentioned that it is a misreading, and that the correct word is *nighl* with a nūn, meaning the base person among people and animals, because the mule does not beget. Ibn Shumayl said: a human being, at the first moment his mother gives birth to him, is called *salīl*. *Salīl* and *salīlah* also mean a young male and female camel (foal).]]

Whoever says: *sulālah* has the plural *sulālāt*, and they sometimes pluralize it as *salāʾil*, though this is not common, because *salāʾil* is the plural of *salīl*. From this is the saying of one of them:

*When the she-camels bring forth their young, they resemble one another in being led, except that their nostrils distinguish their offspring.* [[I did not find this verse in al-Farrāʾ's Maʿānī al-Qurʾān, nor in Abū ʿUbaydah's Majāz al-Qurʾān, nor in the evidence of the lexicon books. It is evidence that *salāʾil* is the plural of *sulālah*, and we have explained its meaning in the two previous pieces of evidence sufficiently to avoid repeating it here.]]

And the saying of the rajaz-poet:

*They cast them out, in their offspring, among the afterbirths.* [[This hemistich appears in the sources in a corrupted form, and the author counted it as rajaz. It seems to me that this is part of a verse of al-Nābighah al-Dhubyānī, which some copyists wrote into certain books, and which the author did not notice. The verse of al-Nābighah is in the *ṭawīl* meter, and it is from a qaṣīdah of his describing horses in the battle of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Aṣghar al-Ghassānī against the Banū Murrah ibn ʿAwf ibn Saʿd ibn Dhubyān, in which he says:

*I have feared, until my fear does not exceed that of a wild goat on the cliff of al-Maṭārah, who is wary.*

*Fearing that ʿAmr's horses might be led against us, between barefoot and shod.*

*When they hasten them away from their natural gait, they strike at their necks with their jaws.*

*And they cast out the foals in every place, writhing in their afterbirths like the striped garments.*

The intended meaning is that the afterbirths were stained with blood. See the verse in (Lisān: sh-ḥ-ṭ), in al-Mukhaṣṣaṣ of Ibn Sīdah (1:17), and in Mukhtār al-Shiʿr al-Jāhilī with the commentary of Muṣṭafā al-Saqqā (Muṣṭafā al-Bābī al-Ḥalabī edition, Cairo, p. 211).]]

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then We made him a sperm-drop in a secure place﴾ (13) ﴿Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump of flesh, then We made the lump of flesh into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ (14)**

Allah, the Exalted, means by His words ﴿Then We made him a sperm-drop in a secure place﴾: Then We made the human being, whom We created from an extract of clay, into a sperm-drop in a secure place, which is the place where the man's sperm settles in the woman's womb. He described it as "secure" because it provides for that and prepares itself for the sperm to settle in it until the time of the matter that He has decreed for it.

* *

As for His words ﴿Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot﴾: He says, Then We transformed the sperm-drop that We had placed in a secure place into a clinging clot, which is a piece of blood. ﴿Then We made the clinging clot into a lump of flesh﴾: He says, Then We made that blood into a lump, which is a piece of flesh.

* *

As for His words ﴿Then We made the lump of flesh into bones﴾: He says, Then We made that lump into bones of flesh. The reciters (qurra') differed in their recitation (qira'ah) of this. The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Iraq, except 'Asim, recited ﴿fa-khalaqna al-mudghata 'izaman﴾ in the plural. 'Asim and 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] recited ﴿'adhman﴾ in the singular in both places.

The recitation that we choose is the plural, because the authoritative reciters are unanimous (ijma') upon it.

* *

As for His words ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾: He says, Then We covered the bones with flesh. It has been mentioned that in the recitation of 'Abdullah it is: "Then We made the lump into bone, and sinew, and We clothed it with flesh."

* *

As for His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾: He says, Then We produced this human being as another creation. The pronoun in ﴿anshha'nahu﴾ refers to the human being mentioned in His words ﴿And We had certainly created man﴾. It is possible that it refers to the bone, the sperm-drop and the lump, making all of that like a single thing, so it is said: Then We produced that as another creation.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the meaning of His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾. Some of them said: His producing him as another creation is His breathing the spirit into him, whereupon he becomes a human being; before that he had been a form.

Mention of those who said this:

Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Hajjaj informed us, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: He breathed the spirit into him.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, from al-Hajjaj ibn Artah, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it.

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: the spirit.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Asbahani, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: He breathed the spirit into him.

Ibn Bashshar and Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, both saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: He breathed the spirit into him.

He said: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: He breathed the spirit into him, and that is the other creation which was mentioned.

I was told from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, meaning the spirit breathed into him after the creation.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words (Then We produced him as another creation), he said: the spirit which He placed in him.

Others said: His producing him as another creation is His transforming him through states after birth, in childhood and in old age, through nourishment, the growth of hair and teeth, and similar states of living beings in this world.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to us, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, he said: He came out from his mother's womb after he had been created; so the beginning of his other creation was that he cried out; then it was part of his creation that he was guided to his mother's breast; then it was part of his creation that he learned how to stretch out his legs until he sat, until he crawled, until he stood on his legs, until he walked, until he was weaned, so he learned how to drink and eat food, until he reached maturity, until he reached the point of moving about in the lands.

Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: Some of them say: it is the growth of hair, and some of them say: it is the breathing of the spirit.

al-Hasan related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

I was told from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: It is said that the other creation is after his coming out of his mother's womb, by his teeth and his hair.

Others said: Rather, by His producing him as another creation He meant: the perfecting of his youth.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, he said: when his youth became complete.

al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Mujahid said: when youth became complete in him.

The most correct of these sayings is the saying of the one who said: He meant by it the breathing of the spirit into him, because by the breathing of the spirit into him he is transformed into another creation, a human being; and before that he was in the states which Allah described him as being in: a sperm-drop, a clot, a lump, and bone; and by the breathing of the spirit into him he is transformed from all those meanings into the meaning of humanity, just as his father Adam was transformed by the breathing of the spirit into the clay from which he was created as a human being, and a creation other than the clay from which he had been created.

* *

As for His words ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾:

The people of interpretation differed regarding its meaning. Some of them said: its meaning is: So blessed is Allah, the best of makers (sani'in).

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam related to us, from 'Anbasah, from Layth, from Mujahid: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, he said: They make, and Allah makes, and Allah is the best of makers.

Others said: It was only said ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ because 'Isa ibn Maryam used to create, so He, may His praise be exalted, informed about Himself that He creates better than what he used to create.

Mention of those who said this:

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, who said: Ibn Juraij said, regarding His words ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, he said: 'Isa ibn Maryam creates.

The most correct of the two sayings is the saying of Mujahid, because the Arabs call every maker a creator (khaliq). Among this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*"And you indeed cut what you have measured out, while others measure but do not cut."*

It is also transmitted as:

*"And you indeed measure what you have cut, while others measure but do not cut."*

[The verse is by Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, praising a man (Lisan al-'Arab: kh-l-q). He says: when you determine a matter, you cut it and carry it out, while others determine what they do not cut, because their resolve is not firm, whereas you are firm in what you have resolved upon. Al-khalq means measuring: one says khalaqa al-adim yakhluquhu khalqan, meaning he measured the leather for what he intends before cutting, and gauged it in order to cut from it a waterskin, a water-container, or a shoe. For this reason the Arabs called every craftsman, such as a carpenter, a tailor and the like, a creator (khaliq), because he measures the wood and determines it according to what he intends for it. Al-fary means cutting after measuring, and it may also be before that, by cutting a piece from a hide or cloth roughly, then adjusting and shaping it by calculation and measurement, according to what he intends. For this reason another transmission of the verse came: "And you indeed measure what you have cut..."]

He says: when you determine a matter, you cut it and carry it out, while others determine what they do not cut, because their resolve is not firm, whereas you are firm in what you have resolved upon. Al-khalq means measuring: one says khalaqa al-adim yakhluquhu khalqan, meaning he measured the leather for what he intends before cutting, and gauged it in order to cut from it a waterskin, a water-container, or a shoe. For this reason the Arabs called every craftsman, such as a carpenter, a tailor and the like, a creator (khaliq), because he measures the wood and determines it according to what he intends for it. Al-fary means cutting after measuring, and it may also be before that, by cutting a piece from a hide or cloth roughly, then adjusting and shaping it by calculation and measurement, according to what he intends. For this reason another transmission of the verse came: "And you indeed measure what you have cut..."]

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed, after that, you will surely die (15). Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised up (16).﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Then indeed you, O people, after your being brought into being as another creation and We have made you a complete human being, will surely die and return to dust as you were. Then indeed, after your death and your return to crumbled, decayed bones, you will be raised from the dust as a new creation, just as We began you the first time.

It was said, ﴿Then indeed, after that, you will surely die﴾, because it is a report about a condition that will come to them and did not yet exist. Likewise the Arabs say of someone who has not yet died: "He is dying (mā'it) and dead (mayyit) soon," but they do not say of someone who has already died "mā'it." Similarly, "he is greedy (ṭam'a) for what is with you" when he is described as greedy; but when it is reported of him that he will do something and has not yet done it, it is said: "he is greedy for what is with you tomorrow." The same applies to everything that is similar to what we have mentioned.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 17:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly created above you seven paths, and We are never unaware of creation.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: "And We have certainly created above you, O people, seven heavens, some above others. The Arabs call everything that is above something else a ṭarīqah (path, layer). The seven heavens are only called seven paths because some of them are above others, so each heaven among them is a ṭarīqah."

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said something similar to what we have said regarding the interpretation of this.

Those who said that:

* Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding the saying of God: ﴿And We have certainly created above you seven paths﴾, "The ṭarā'iq (paths) are the heavens."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿and We are never unaware of creation﴾

It means: "And We were not unaware, in Our creating the seven heavens above you, of Our creation that is beneath them. Rather, We were guarding them from the fall of the heavens upon them, which would destroy them."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 18–19:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We caused it to settle in the earth; and indeed, We are able to take it away.﴾ (18)

His, may He be exalted and remembered, saying: And We sent down from the sky water that is in the earth, so We caused it to settle there.

As has been reported:

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We caused it to settle in the earth﴾ — water that comes from the sky.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are able to take it away﴾

He, may His praise be exalted, says: And indeed We are able to take away the water that We caused to settle in the earth, so that you, O people, would perish of thirst, your land would be ruined, so that it would not produce crops or plantations, and your livestock would perish. He means: among the favors I have bestowed upon you is My leaving it for you flowing in the earth.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿So We produced for you thereby gardens of palm trees and grapevines; in them you have abundant fruits, and from them you eat﴾ (19)

His, may He be exalted and remembered, saying: So We brought into being for you, by means of the water that We sent down from the sky, gardens of palm trees and grapevines. ﴿For you therein﴾ means: for you in the gardens are abundant fruits. ﴿And from them you eat﴾ means: and from the fruits you eat. It is permissible that the pronoun ("ha'" and "alif") refers to the gardens, and it may also refer to the palm trees and grapevines. God, may His praise be exalted, specified the gardens He mentioned in this place by describing them as consisting of palm trees and grapevines, rather than describing them by all the other fruits of the earth; because these two kinds of fruit were the greatest fruits of the Hijaz and its vicinity. Palm trees belonged to the people of Madinah, and grapevines to the people of al-Ta'if. So He reminded the people of what they knew of God's favor upon them, through the fruits He bestowed upon them from these.

The commentary on the verse: "And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, producing oil and a condiment for those who eat" (23:20)

Al-Tabari said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "We also produced for you a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai," and the tree is in the accusative, coordinated with the gardens (al-jannat), and by it He means the olive tree (shajarat al-zaytun).

* *

As for His words, "that springs forth from Mount Sinai" (takhruju min Tur Sayna'),

it means: it springs forth from a mountain that produces trees.

I have already explained the meaning of al-Tur (the mountain) earlier, with its evidence, and the differing views of those who differ have made it unnecessary to repeat it here.

As for "Sayna'," the reciters differed in its reading. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra read it "Sīnā'" with a kasra on the sin, while the majority of the reciters of Kufa read it "Saynā'" with a fatha on the sin. Both readings agree on the lengthening of the alif (madd).

The correct view on this is that they are two well-known readings among the recitations of the major cities (amsar), with the same meaning, so whichever of them the reciter reads is correct.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about its explanation. Some of them said: its meaning is "the blessed," as if the sense of the statement, in their view, is: "and a tree that springs forth from a blessed mountain."

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words "Tur Sayna'," he said: "the blessed."

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words "and a tree that springs forth from Tur Sayna'," he said: "It is a mountain in Syria, blessed."

Others said: its meaning is "good."

Those who said this:

- Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning His words "Tur Sayna'," he said: "It is a good mountain."

- I was told from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His words "min Tur Sayna'": "al-Tur: the mountain in Nabataean (al-Nabatiyya); and Sayna': 'good' in Nabataean."

Others said: it is the name of a well-known mountain.

Those who said this:

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata' al-Khurasani, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words "min Tur Sayna'," he said: "The mountain from which Musa ﷺ was called."

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words "Tur Sayna'," he said: "It is the mountain of Tur which is in Syria, a mountain in Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis); he said: it is extended, it lies between Egypt and Aylah."

Others said: its meaning is that it is a mountain with trees.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from one who said it.

The correct view on this is to say: Sayna' is a name to which al-Tur is added, by which it is known, just as it is said "Jabalay Tayy'," which are added to Tayy'. If the matter were as those who said "its meaning is a blessed mountain" said, or as those who said "its meaning is good" said, then al-Tur would be nunated (tanwin), and the word Sayna' would be its adjective. Furthermore, Sayna' in the sense of "blessed" or "good" is not known in the speech of the Arabs, so that it could be made an attribute of the mountain. Rather, the correct view, God willing, is as Ibn Abbas said: that it is a mountain known by that name, and that it is the mountain from which Musa ﷺ was called, and it is also blessed, not that the meaning of Sayna' is "blessed."

* *

As for His words, "it springs forth with oil" (tanbutu bi'l-duhn),

the reciters differed in reading "tunbitu." The majority of the reciters of the major cities read "tanbutu" with a fatha on the ta', meaning: this tree grows with the fruit of oil. Some reciters of Basra read "tunbitu" with a damma on the ta', meaning: it causes the oil to grow, produces it. It is reported that in the reading of Abd Allah it is "tukhriju al-duhn" (it produces the oil). They said: the ba' in this place is superfluous (za'ida), as it is said: "akhadhtu thawbahu" and "akhadhtu bi-thawbihi," and as the rajiz said:

"We are the sons of Ja'dah, lords of al-Falaj... we strike with the white swords and hope for relief (bi-l-faraj)."

[The line is by Nabigha of Banu Ja'dah (Khizanat al-Adab by al-Baghdadi, 4:160). Al-Falaj originally means a small river and flowing water; the intended meaning in the line is a place in the high lands of Qays. It is also related as "nadribu bi's-sayf." Al-Bid: plural of abyad, meaning the sword. The line is evidence for the superfluity of the ba' in "bi'l-faraj," i.e., "wa-narju al-faraj." It is superfluous in the direct object by transmitted usage (sama'an). Ibn Usfur said in al-Darura'if: the superfluity of the ba' here is a poetic necessity (darura). Ibn al-Sayyid said in his commentary on Ibn Qutaybah's Adab al-Katib: the verb "raja" was made to govern with "ba'" because it means "tama'" (desire), which governs with "ba'," as you say "tama'tu bi-kadha." The poet said: "I desired Layla that she might be generous, but desires only sever the necks of men." Banu Ja'dah may be read in the nominative as the predicate of "nahnu," or in the accusative as a specification (ikhtisas), with the predicate being "arbab." End.]

Meaning: "and we hope for relief." My view on this is that they are two dialects: nabata and anbata. From the one who used anbata is the saying of Zuhayr:

"You saw the owners of needs around their houses, dependants with them, until the herbage sprouted (anbata al-baql)."

[The line is in Lisan al-Arab (nabata). It says: nabata al-baql and anbata are the same in meaning, and it cites Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma: "When the white year (al-sanat al-shahba') afflicted the people, and the noble among the people were struck by the calamity of the year..." He then said: "al-shahba'" means the white, i.e., the barren drought, because it whitens with snow or the absence of growth. "Al-hajrah" is the severe year which confines people in their houses, so that they slaughter their noble camels to eat them. "Al-qatin" are the household and the inhabitants of the house. "Ajhafat" harmed them and destroyed their wealth. He said: nabata and anbata are like their saying "matarat al-sama'" and "amtarat." He said regarding His words "tanbutu bi'l-duhn": Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr al-Hadrami read "tunbitu" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ba'. Nafi', Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Amir read with a fatha on the ta'. al-Farra' said: they are two dialects: nabatat al-ardu and anbatat. Ibn Sida said: as for "tunbitu" (with damma on the ta'), many people went to the view that its meaning is "tunbitu al-duhn," i.e., the tree of oil, or the seed of oil, and that the ba' in it is superfluous, as is the verse of 'Antarah "shariba bi-ma' al-Dahrada'in..." They said he meant "shariba ma' al-Dahrada'in." He said: this, according to the expert among our companions, is not in the sense of superfluity, but its interpretation, God knows best, is: it causes to grow what it causes to grow with the oil in it, as you say: "Zayd went out with his garments on him," and "the amir rode with his sword," i.e., and his sword with him. End.]

It is also transmitted as "nabata," and it is like His words "fa-asri bi-ahlika" and "fa-sir," except that, although this is so, the reading which I do not choose other than is the reading of him who reads "tanbutu" with a fatha on the ta', because the reciters, as an authoritative consensus (ijma' al-hujjah), agree upon it. Its meaning is: this tree grows with the fruit of oil.

As:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "tanbutu bi'l-duhn," he said: "with its fruit."

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

The oil which is from its fruit is olive oil.

As:

- Ali related to me, saying: Abd Allah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words "tanbutu bi'l-duhn," he said: "It is the oil which is eaten and with which one anoints."

* *

As for His words, "and a condiment for those who eat" (wa-sibghin li'l-akilin),

he says: it grows with oil and with a condiment for those who eat, those who dip (yasta bighu) with the olive oil which they eat.

As:

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words "wa-sibghin li'l-akilin": "This olive is a condiment for those who eat, they season their food with it, and dip with it."

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: so "sibgh" is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "duhn."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 21–22:

On the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ (21).

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿And indeed, for you﴾ O people, ﴿in the cattle there is a lesson﴾ by which you take heed, so that you may recognise through them God's favours upon you and His power over what He wills, and that He is the One whom nothing He wills can escape, and nothing He desires can overcome. ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾ of the milk that comes out from between the digested matter and the blood. ﴿And for you﴾ besides that

﴿in them﴾, meaning in the cattle, ﴿are many benefits﴾, such as the camels upon which loads are carried, whose backs are ridden, and whose milk is drunk. ﴿And from them you eat﴾, meaning you eat of their meat.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ (22).

He says: upon the cattle and upon the ships you are carried; upon these on land, and upon those at sea.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 21–22:

On the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ (21).

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿And indeed, for you﴾ O people, ﴿in the cattle there is a lesson﴾ by which you take heed, so that you may recognise through them God's favours upon you and His power over what He wills, and that He is the One whom nothing He wills can escape, and nothing He desires can overcome. ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾ of the milk that comes out from between the digested matter and the blood. ﴿And for you﴾ besides that

﴿in them﴾, meaning in the cattle, ﴿are many benefits﴾, such as the camels upon which loads are carried, whose backs are ridden, and whose milk is drunk. ﴿And from them you eat﴾, meaning you eat of their meat.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ (22).

He says: upon the cattle and upon the ships you are carried; upon these on land, and upon those at sea.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verses 23–27:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear [Him]?"﴾ (23)

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾, calling them to obey Us and to affirm Our oneness and to disavow every object of worship other than Us. ﴿And he said﴾ to them, Noah: ﴿O my people, worship Allah﴾, meaning: he said to them, "Submit, O my people, to Allah in obedience." ﴿You have no deity other than Him﴾, meaning: you have no object of worship that it is permissible for you to worship besides Him. ﴿Will you not then fear [Him]?﴾, meaning: will you not fear, by worshipping other than Him, His punishment befalling you?

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿So the eminent ones who disbelieved among his people said, "This is not but a man like yourselves who wants to make himself superior over you. And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our forefathers of old.﴾ (24)

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: the group of nobles of Noah's people, those who denied the oneness of Allah and called him a liar to their people, said: "Noah is, O people, only a man like you; he is nothing but a human being like you and like some of you," ﴿who wants to make himself superior over you﴾, meaning: who wants to have superiority over you, so that he would be followed and you would be his followers. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, meaning: and if Allah had willed that we not worship anything besides Him, He would have sent down angels; that is, He would have sent angels to deliver to you his message, conveying with the call to what Noah calls you to.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿We have not heard of this﴾,

that which Noah calls us to, namely that there is no deity for us other than Allah, in the past centuries, which are their forefathers of old.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿He is not but a man in whom is madness, so wait for him for a time.﴾ (25) ﴿[Noah] said, "My Lord, support me because they have denied me."﴾ (26) ﴿So We revealed to him, "Construct the ship under Our eyes and Our inspiration. And when Our command comes and the oven overflows, insert into it of each kind two mates and your family, except those among them about whom the word has already preceded. And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned."﴾ (27)

He, may He be exalted and remembered, means, reporting the saying of the eminent ones who disbelieved among Noah's people: ﴿He is not but a man in whom is madness﴾, meaning: Noah is only a man with madness. It may also be said of the jinn: "janna," so the noun and the verbal noun agree; and it comes from His saying: ﴿He is not﴾, referring to the name of Noah.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿So wait for him for a time﴾,

it means: remain with him and wait for him until a time, meaning: until some time; they did not intend by that a known time, but it is like the saying of the speaker: "Leave him until some day," or "until some time." His saying: ﴿[Noah] said, "My Lord, support me because they have denied me."﴾ means: Noah said, calling upon his Lord, seeking help from Him against his people, when his affair and theirs had lengthened and they persisted in their error: ﴿My Lord, support me﴾ against my people ﴿because they have denied me﴾, meaning by their denial of me in what I conveyed of Your message and called them to of Your oneness.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿So We revealed to him, "Construct the ship under Our eyes and Our inspiration"﴾,

it means: We said to him when We had granted him help against the disbelievers of his people: construct the ship, which is the boat, under Our eyes, meaning: in Our sight and view, and Our inspiration, meaning: by Our teaching you its construction. ﴿And when Our command comes﴾, meaning: when Our decree concerning your people comes, with their punishment and destruction, ﴿and the oven overflows﴾.

We have previously mentioned the differences of those who differ regarding the description of the overflowing of the oven. The correct view in our opinion concerning it, with its evidences, suffices so that it need not be repeated in this place.

﴿Then insert into it of each kind two mates﴾, meaning: enter into the ship and carry. The ha and alif in His saying ﴿into it﴾ refer to the ship. ﴿Of each kind two mates﴾. It is said: "salaktuhu fi kadha" and "aslaktuhu fihi," and of "salaktuhu" is the saying of the poet:

"And I was a tenacious opponent of yours, not fleeing, / while they had made you enter a grievous day."

[The verse is by Adi ibn Zayd al-Ibadi; the author cited it elsewhere, and here as evidence that one says "salaktuhu fi kadha," meaning "I made him enter it."]

Some say "asjaktu" with an alif, and from it is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"Until when they made them enter into Qutaidah, / they drove them away as the camel-herders drive the stray ones."

[The verse is by Abd Manaf ibn Rabi al-Hudhali; the author cited it earlier as evidence of the usage "aslakahu fihi."]

And in accordance with what we have said about this, the people of interpretation spoke.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, he said: my father related to me, he said: my uncle related to me, he said: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Then insert into it of each kind two mates﴾, he says to Noah: put in the ship of each kind two mates, ﴿and your family﴾, namely his sons and their wives, ﴿except those about whom the word has already preceded﴾ from Allah that they are doomed among those of your people who will perish, so do not carry them with you; and he is Yam, who drowned.

By His saying ﴿among them﴾ he means from among the family; the ha and mim in His saying ﴿among them﴾ refer to the family.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And do not address Me﴾,

the verse means: do not ask Me concerning those who disbelieved in Allah that I should save them.

﴿Indeed, they are to be drowned﴾, meaning: for I have decreed upon them that I drown all of them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verses 23–27:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear [Him]?"﴾ (23)

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ (29) ﴿Indeed, in that are signs, and indeed We were ever testing.﴾ (30)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Noah, peace be upon him: And say, when Allah has brought you safely and taken you out of the ship, and you have descended from it: ﴿"My Lord, cause me to land"﴾ from the earth ﴿"at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the like of what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿a blessed landing place﴾: for Noah, when he descended from the ship.

- Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the reciters of the metropolitan cities read ﴿Rabbi anzilni munzalan mubarakan﴾ with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the zay, meaning: "cause me to descend a blessed descent." Asim read ﴿manzalan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the zay, meaning: "cause me to descend to a blessed place and station."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Indeed, in what We did to the people of Noah, O Muhammad, when We destroyed them because they denied Our messengers, rejected Our oneness, and worshipped gods and idols, there are lessons for your people among the polytheists of Quraysh, admonitions and proofs from Us by which they may draw inference regarding Our way with the likes of them, so that they desist from their disbelief and refrain from denying you, fearing that there may befall them the like of the punishment that befell those people.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed We were ever testing﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: And We were testing them by reminding them of Our signs, so that We might see what they would do before Our punishment descended upon them.

He, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Noah, peace be upon him: And say, when Allah has brought you safely and taken you out of the ship, and you have descended from it: ﴿"My Lord, cause me to land"﴾ from the earth ﴿"at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the like of what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿a blessed landing place﴾: for Noah, when he descended from the ship.

- Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the reciters of the metropolitan cities read ﴿Rabbi anzilni munzalan mubarakan﴾ with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the zay, meaning: "cause me to descend a blessed descent." Asim read ﴿manzalan﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the zay, meaning: "cause me to descend to a blessed place and station."

* *

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: And We were testing them by reminding them of Our signs, so that We might see what they would do before Our punishment descended upon them.

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then We produced after them another generation﴾ (31) ﴿and We sent among them a Messenger from among themselves, [saying]: "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ (32)

He, exalted is He, says: Then We brought into being after the destruction of the people of Noah another generation, and We created them. ﴿And We sent among them a Messenger from among themselves﴾ calling them [to the truth], ﴿saying: "Worship Allah"﴾ O my people, and obey Him rather than the gods and idols, for worship is fitting only for Him. ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ means: you have no worshipped deity worthy of being worshipped besides Him. ﴿Will you not then fear Him?﴾ means: will you not fear the punishment of Allah for worshipping anything besides Him, when He is the God for whom you have no god besides Him?

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿But the chiefs of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the life of this world, said: "This is none but a human being like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink.﴾ (33)

He, exalted is He, says: The nobles of the people of the Messenger whom We sent after Noah said this. By "the Messenger" in this place is meant Salih, and by "his people" are meant Thamud. ﴿Who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ means: those who rejected the Oneness of Allah and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, i.e., they denied the meeting with Allah in the Hereafter.

As for His words: ﴿and whom We had given luxury in the life of this world﴾

This means: We granted them ease in their worldly life by widening their livelihood for them and extending provision to them, until they grew insolent and transgressed against their Lord and disbelieved. From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"And indeed I have seen myself in the abodes, pampered [mutrafan]..." [[The verse is by al-Ajjaj (Arajiz al-Arab, edited by al-Sayyid Muhammad Tawfiq al-Bakri, p. 19). In Lisan al-Arab (root t-r-f): "Al-mutraf: one who is pampered, who has expanded in the pleasures and desires of the world. Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verses 34–35:

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, indeed you would then be losers﴾ [34] ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [35]

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, reporting the words of the chiefs of the people of Salih to their people: ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves﴾, following him, accepting what he says and believing him. ﴿Indeed you, O people, would then be losers﴾. He says: they said, "Indeed you would then be deprived (maghbunun) of your shares of honour and eminence in this world by following him."

* *

His saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones...﴾

The verse. He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: they said to them, "Does Salih promise you that when you have died and are dust in your graves, and bones whose flesh has gone and whose bones remain, you will be brought out of your graves alive, as you were before your death?" The words ﴿that you﴾ are repeated twice, and the meaning is: "Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought out (once only)?" Because the first ﴿that you﴾ was separated from its predicate by "when" (idha), and so the Arabs do with every noun that the verb of thinking (zann) and its sisters govern, when a conditional clause interposes before its predicate: they repeat its noun once and omit it another time. So you say: "I think that if you sit with us, you are good (anna-ka muhsin)." If you omit the first or the second "that you," it is acceptable; if you keep both, it is acceptable too. But if nothing is interposed between them, it is not permissible to say, "I think that you that you are sitting." It is mentioned that this is in the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth﴾ ...

Ahl al-ta'wil (the scholars of interpretation) said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

◆ Ali related to me, he said: Abdullah related to us, he said: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Far, far⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ — he says: far, far away.

◆ Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿Far, far is that which you are promised﴾. He said: It means the resurrection. The Arabs attach the lam to hayhat (hayhata, an interjection meaning "far") with the noun that accompanies it and remove it from it. They say: hayhat laka (far for you), hayhata ma tabtaghi (far is what you seek). When the lam is dropped, they raise the noun, in the sense of hayhat, as if he said: far is what is fitting for you; as Jarir said:

*Fa-hayhata hayhat al-'aqiq wa man bihi … wa-hayhata khillun bil-'aqiq nuwasiluhu*

[The verse is by Jarir ibn Atiyya al-Khatafi (Lisan al-Arab: h-y-h). The narration in it is: "al-'Aqiq wa-ahluhu" ("al-'Aqiq and its people"), and in the Diwan (Sawi edition, p. 479): "Fa-ayhata ayhata al-'Aqiq wa man bihi … wa-ayhata wasl bil-'Aqiq nuwasiluhu".

It is from a qasida in which he replies to al-Farazdaq. Al-'Aqiq: a valley of the Banu Kilab, transmitted by al-Bakri in Mu'jam ma Ista'jam from Imara ibn Aqil. Hayhat and ayhat: a word meaning distance; it is said hayhat is a word expressing distance. Jarir said: "Fa-hayhat…" (the verse). The ta' is open, like kayfa, and its origin is a ha'; some people vocalize it with a kasra in every case. Humayd al-Artat, describing camels that had crossed lands until they reached the deserts, said: *Hayhata man musbihuha hayhat … hayhat hajrun min sunaybi'at*.]

He said: the lam is attached to hayhat as a noun because they said hayhat is a particle not derived from a verb; so they attached the lam to it, just as they attached it to halumma (come on), since it is not derived from a verb. When they say aqbil (come), they do not say laka, because the verb admits a pronoun of the noun.

The scholars of Arabic differed over how to pause on hayhat. Al-Kisa'i preferred pausing on it with a ha', because it is in the accusative case; al-Farra' preferred pausing with a ta', and said: some Arabs vocalize the ta' with a kasra, which shows it is not the ta' of feminine marking; so it is like dara*k* and nazzar. As for the fatha on the ta' in both, it is because they are two particles, so they are like khamsata 'ashar (fifteen). Al-Farra' said: if it is said that each one is self-sufficient, it is permissible to pause on it, and its fatha is like the fatha in his saying: thumma jalasa (then he sat); and like the poet's saying:

*Mawiyya ya rubbatama gharatin … sh'waa ka-l-lad'ati bil-misam*

[The verse is in (Lisan: h-y-h, r-b-b). In the second, he said: the difference between rubbama and rubba is that rubba is followed only by a noun, whereas rubbama has ma added to rubba so that a verb can follow it; one says: rubba rajulin ja'ani, and rubbama ja'ani Zayd, and likewise rubbatama. Ibn al-A'rabi recited "Mawiyya…" etc. Al-Kisa'i said: I think they refrained from making the ba' of rubba quiescent because the ta' of feminine marking enters it often, as in their saying rubbat rajul. He means that the ta' of feminine marking is never preceded by anything but a fatha or what is intended as a fatha; since the ta' of feminine marking enters it often, they refrained from making quiescent the letter before the ha' of feminine marking, and preferred the fatha (meaning by naṣb, fatha). End quote. He said in sh-'-a: "ash'a al-qawm al-ghara" means they set the raid alight, and a ghara shawa' is a scattered widespread raid. Ibn al-A'rabi recited the verse "Mawiyya…": al-misam means the branding iron, or the thing with which animals are branded; its plural is mawasim and mayasim.]

He said: so hayhat is given the fatha like this ha' in rubbata, because it entered upon a particle, upon rubb and upon thumma, and these were particles, and it did not change them from their particle status, so they were given the fatha.

The readers differed in reading this. The readers of the major cities other than Abu Ja'far read ﴿hayhāta hayhāta﴾ with a fatha on the ta' in both. Abu Ja'far read ﴿hayhāti hayhāti﴾ with a kasra on the ta' in both. The fatha in both is the reading we hold, because the consensus of the authoritative readers is upon it.

And His saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world﴾

He says: there is no life except our life of this world in which we are, ﴿we die and we live﴾ — he says: the living among us die and do not live again, and others among us come into being and are born alive ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾ — he says: they said: we will not be resurrected after death.

As:

◆ Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected﴾. He said: he says there is no afterlife nor resurrection; they deny the resurrection, saying: there is only this life of ours, then we die and do not live; these die and those live; they say: people are like crops, this one is harvested and that one grows; they say: these die and others come. And he recited: ﴿And those who disbelieve said: Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you when you are completely torn apart that you will be in a new creation?﴾ And he recited: ﴿The Hour will not come upon us. Say: Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you﴾.

It is from a qasida in which he replies to al-Farazdaq. Al-'Aqiq: a valley of the Banu Kilab, transmitted by al-Bakri in Mu'jam ma Ista'jam from Imara ibn Aqil. Hayhat and ayhat: a word meaning distance; it is said hayhat is a word expressing distance. Jarir said: "Fa-hayhat…" (the verse). The ta' is open, like kayfa, and its origin is a ha'; some people vocalize it with a kasra in every case. Humayd al-Artat, describing camels that had crossed lands until they reached the deserts, said: *Hayhata man musbihuha hayhat … hayhat hajrun min sunaybi'at*.]

He said: the lam is attached to hayhat as a noun because they said hayhat is a particle not derived from a verb; so they attached the lam to it, just as they attached it to halumma (come on), since it is not derived from a verb. When they say aqbil (come), they do not say laka, because the verb admits a pronoun of the noun.

The scholars of Arabic differed over how to pause on hayhat. Al-Kisa'i preferred pausing on it with a ha', because it is in the accusative case; al-Farra' preferred pausing with a ta', and said: some Arabs vocalize the ta' with a kasra, which shows it is not the ta' of feminine marking; so it is like dara*k* and nazzar. As for the fatha on the ta' in both, it is because they are two particles, so they are like khamsata 'ashar (fifteen). Al-Farra' said: if it is said that each one is self-sufficient, it is permissible to pause on it, and its fatha is like the fatha in his saying: thumma jalasa (then he sat); and like the poet's saying:

*Mawiyya ya rubbatama gharatin … sh'waa ka-l-lad'ati bil-misam*

[The verse is in (Lisan: h-y-h, r-b-b). In the second, he said: the difference between rubbama and rubba is that rubba is followed only by a noun, whereas rubbama has ma added to rubba so that a verb can follow it; one says: rubba rajulin ja'ani, and rubbama ja'ani Zayd, and likewise rubbatama. Ibn al-A'rabi recited "Mawiyya…" etc. Al-Kisa'i said: I think they refrained from making the ba' of rubba quiescent because the ta' of feminine marking enters it often, as in their saying rubbat rajul. He means that the ta' of feminine marking is never preceded by anything but a fatha or what is intended as a fatha; since the ta' of feminine marking enters it often, they refrained from making quiescent the letter before the ha' of feminine marking, and preferred the fatha (meaning by naṣb, fatha). End quote. He said in sh-'-a: "ash'a al-qawm al-ghara" means they set the raid alight, and a ghara shawa' is a scattered widespread raid. Ibn al-A'rabi recited the verse "Mawiyya…": al-misam means the branding iron, or the thing with which animals are branded; its plural is mawasim and mayasim.]

He said: so hayhat is given the fatha like this ha' in rubbata, because it entered upon a particle, upon rubb and upon thumma, and these were particles, and it did not change them from their particle status, so they were given the fatha.

The readers differed in reading this. The readers of the major cities other than Abu Ja'far read ﴿hayhāta hayhāta﴾ with a fatha on the ta' in both. Abu Ja'far read ﴿hayhāti hayhāti﴾ with a kasra on the ta' in both. The fatha in both is the reading we hold, because the consensus of the authoritative readers is upon it.

And His saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world﴾

He says: there is no life except our life of this world in which we are, ﴿we die and we live﴾ — he says: the living among us die and do not live again, and others among us come into being and are born alive ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾ — he says: they said: we will not be resurrected after death.

As:

◆ Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected﴾. He said: he says there is no afterlife nor resurrection; they deny the resurrection, saying: there is only this life of ours, then we die and do not live; these die and those live; they say: people are like crops, this one is harvested and that one grows; they say: these die and others come. And he recited: ﴿And those who disbelieve said: Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you when you are completely torn apart that you will be in a new creation?﴾ And he recited: ﴿The Hour will not come upon us. Say: Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verses 38–41:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿It is only a man who has invented a lie against God, and we will not believe him﴾ (38). ﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, because they have denied me"﴾ (39). ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful"﴾ (40).

His, the Exalted's, meaning: They said that Salih was only a man who fabricated a lie against God, in his saying ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾, and in his promise to you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth.

* *

As for His words ﴿he﴾:

It refers to the Messenger, who is Salih. ﴿And we will not believe him﴾ means: we will not believe him in what he says, that we have no god other than God, and in what he promises us of resurrection after death.

* *

As for His words ﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, because they have denied me"﴾:

It means: Salih said, when he despaired of his people's faith in God and of their believing him by their saying ﴿and we will not believe him﴾: "My Lord, help me against these people because of their denial of me", meaning: because of their denying me regarding what I have called them to of the truth. So peace be upon him sought help from his Lord against their harm to him and their denial of him. God said to him, responding to his request and to what he asked: "In a little while, O Salih, your denying people from your nation will surely become regretful for their denial of you", and that will be when Our punishment descends upon them, and regret will not benefit them.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿So the Cry seized them in truth, and We made them debris. So away with the wrongdoing people﴾ (41).

His, the Exalted's, meaning: So We took vengeance upon them, sending upon them the Cry, which seized them in truth, because God punished them by their deserving punishment from Him for their disbelief in Him and their denial of His Messenger. ﴿And We made them debris (ghuthaʾ)﴾ means: We made them like debris (ghuthaʾ), which is what rises upon the flood and the like, which is of no benefit for anything. This is an example, and the meaning is: We destroyed them and made them like something of no benefit.

The people of interpretation have said similarly to what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And We made them debris, so away with the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning: they were made like dead, decayed wood.

It means: God put far away the disbelieving people by their destruction, since they disbelieved in their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and wronged themselves.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 23, verses 42–43:

The meaning of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Then We produced after them other generations(42) No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay it.(43)﴾

He, may He be remembered, says: Then We brought into being, after the destruction of Thamud, other people.

* *

And His words: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term﴾

He says: No destruction of any nation among those peoples whom We produced after Thamud precedes the term We appointed for its destruction, nor is its destruction delayed beyond the term We appointed for it and the time We fixed for its perishing; rather, it is destroyed when that time comes. This is a warning from God to the polytheists of the people of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and an announcement from Him to them that His deferring their terms, despite their disbelief in Him and their denial of His Messenger, is so that they may reach the term appointed for them, whereupon His vengeance will descend upon them, in accordance with His practice toward those before them from the earlier nations.
